title: Expanding clinical research efficiency through intelligent data flow: The IgniteData approach to healthcare innovation
summary: Clinical research teams spend significant time and resources manually transcribing data into study systems, a process that’s labor intensive, error prone, and a major driver of cost and delays in clinical trials. IgniteData's innovative solution eliminates that bottleneck entirely, automating the flow of research-ready clinical data, providing: Learn how modern clinical data standards and digital approaches drive innovation in clinical research, helping sponsors and providers deliver more reliable, faster study results and better patient outcomes.
body_text: This is part of a series: Brief interviews with healthcare innovators Welcome to our “ Brief interviews with healthcare innovators ” series highlighting the cutting-edge companies in the Labcorp Venture Fund portfolio. The mission of the Labcorp Venture Fund is to strategically invest in innovative businesses making healthcare more personalized, accessible, and convenient. These innovators use technology to satisfy their mission of improving health system operations and patient experiences while simplifying and reducing the growing duties of physicians, healthcare staff, and administrators. This month, Kristen Andrews, head of research site enablement at Labcorp, interviewed Zach Taft, CEO of IgniteData , to discuss the company's mission, innovative solutions, and measurable impact. Labcorp is proud to be an investor in IgniteData, a groundbreaking platform that automates the flow of clinical data from source directly into sponsor systems, eliminating the manual bottlenecks that slow clinical trials and delay patient access to potentially lifesaving treatments. Their technology allows research sites and sponsors to collaborate with greater speed, accuracy, and confidence, reflecting our shared commitment to advancing clinical research so breakthrough therapies reach patients faster. IgniteData was founded in 2014 with the mission to make hospital-to-sponsor clinical data flow speedy, reliable, and research-ready so studies can run smarter and faster. “We’re excited to invest in IgniteData so we can help them deliver smarter, faster studies and better patient outcomes.” – Kristen Andrews, Head of Research Site Enablement, Labcorp Origination of innovation Kristen Andrews: Tell us the founding story of IgniteData and its mission. Zach Taft: IgniteData was founded with a straightforward but powerful ambition: unlock healthcare data that’s often trapped in electronic health record (EHR) systems and put it to work improving clinical research and patient outcomes. Our founders, Rich Yeatman and Dan Hydes, were initially inspired by observing the data silos and inefficiencies involved in running clinical trials at large research hospitals, particularly the challenges of accessing and transferring high-quality data. In the company's early years, we built a highly successful patient-recruitment business, helping sponsors enroll thousands of patients into clinical trials. That work gave us deep insight into how research operates in the real world and led to partnerships supporting real-world evidence studies with major life science organizations. Time and again, however, the same fundamental bottleneck surfaced: transferring high-quality clinical data from hospitals to research teams was slow, manual, unreliable, and error prone. By 2019, the ecosystem was ready for change. Emerging interoperability standards, evolving regulation, and growing acceptance of secure cloud-based software made it possible to build something genuinely new. Early validation with partners including AstraZeneca and University College London Hospitals proved our approach, while a codevelopment partnership with Memorial Sloan Kettering (MSK) Cancer Center helped accelerate our platform in one of the world's leading clinical research environments. Today, our mission is simple but powerful: enable seamless hospital-to-sponsor data flow so clinical trials can run faster, more efficiently, and with higher-quality data. Kristen Andrews: What was the inspiration behind starting this venture? Zach Taft: The inspiration is both personal and professional. Our founders, Rich and Dan, each lost their mothers to cancer. I also lost my mother at a young age. What began as a deeply personal commitment to improving outcomes for patients through better clinical research evolved into a professional calling for all of us. At the same time, our collective experience in technology, healthcare operations, and research made it clear that many barriers in clinical trials are avoidable. We’re united by the belief that progress in research matters and it shouldn’t be slowed by: Technology Manual processes Avoidable barriers Fragmented data Operational inefficiencies Therapeutic area Our purpose is to remove friction from clinical research to help the healthcare ecosystem deliver smarter, faster studies and better outcomes for patients. New technology in healthcare Kristen Andrews: What specific problems in the healthcare system does IgniteData address? Zach Taft: We address a major inefficiency at the intersection of healthcare and clinical research: the manual, time-consuming process of re-entering patient data from EHRs into research systems. Research teams spend countless hours transcribing information that already exists in the EHR, leading to: Delays Higher costs Data-quality issues Staff burnout Limited site participation Every single day that data is delayed represents a $1-$8 million opportunity cost to the sponsor. By eliminating weeks from each data transfer, we unlock significant opportunities for pharmaceutical companies to de-risk those costly delays and connect patients with viable opportunities faster. Kristen Andrews: Describe your innovative solution and how it works in practice. Zach Taft: Our core solution, Archer, connects directly into a site's existing source for a simple implementation that can be completed in less than 90 minutes, although broader organizational onboarding may take a few weeks. Once live, Archer automates the flow of clinical data from the source to sponsor using modern interoperability standards such as HL7 FHIR and API-driven integrations. It maps study-specific data to source fields and continuously extracts relevant information as care is delivered, sending it directly into the sponsor's system with full traceability back to the source. The results are measurable: 99.999% data accuracy 6.8 times faster movement of data 87.15% reduction in data queries Faster study execution Research staff are freed from transcription work to focus on patient care, while sponsors gain faster, higher-quality data to drive study execution. Kristen Andrews: What makes Archer unique compared to existing alternatives? Zach Taft: The platform is built with a singular focus on quality and efficiency. We’re not trying to do everything. We’re focused on one critical problem and solving it at scale. However, three things set us apart. 1. It’s system agnostic. Archer works across different health systems, research platforms, and sponsor environments without requiring organizations to adopt a specific technology stack. Archer can accept data inputs from any source and transfer data outputs to any sponsor system. No other tool delivers full agnosticism, making us flexible and uniquely accessible to all sites and sponsors globally. 2. It doesn’t store patient data. Archer acts as a secure, real-time conduit that moves data from source to destination with full traceability, simplifying compliance and meeting HIPAA, GDPR, GCP, and other regulatory requirements worldwide, all while not persisting any patient data. This reduces risk and simplifies adoption. 3. It has a premium site network. Archer’s proven success has resulted in a rapidly growing network of top-ranked, global sites. More than 80% of National Cancer Institute–designated clinical research sites, including eight of the top 10 ranked cancer institutions, are engaging with Archer and prioritize sponsors engaged with IgniteData. How technological innovation improved operations and patient outcomes Kristen Andrews: How has Archer improved patient care and operational efficiency in hospitals and health systems? Zach Taft: Within hospitals and health systems, our primary users are clinical research coordinators. Before Archer, these teams spent a significant portion of their time manually transcribing and validating data, a process that’s error prone and a well-documented source of frustration and burnout. Archer automates that work, allowing coordinators to focus on patient-facing activities, data review, and study management. Coordinators report a satisfaction score of 92%, most commonly citing usability, data quality, and their collaborative experience with IgniteData as primary sources of satisfaction. By reducing data-transfer durations from 30 days down to three, we’re connecting patients with data-driven decisions in near real time, allowing sponsors to expand or suspend trials based on confirmed outcomes. In 2025, we saw a: 676% increase in enrolled patients More than 10-fold increase in exported data points 489% increase in live studies For health systems, this translates into increased capacity and more sustainable research operations. Sites can run more studies in parallel, which also expands patient access to clinical trials. For sponsors, faster and higher-quality data assists better decision-making. Reducing delays in data access can significantly reduce the cost of clinical trials, where each day of delay can represent millions of dollars in opportunity cost . From a patient perspective, faster data flow means quicker insights, more responsive trials, and improved access to innovative treatments. Kristen Andrews: Can you share a case study that demonstrates your impact? Zach Taft: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center is our most comprehensive and long-standing example. Through a codevelopment partnership , MSK has enabled Archer across approximately 60 studies, automatically transferring more than 150,000 clinical data points directly from the EHR into sponsor and investigator research systems. In a timed validation, Archer-supported data entry was 58% faster and 99% less error prone than manual abstraction, and research staff expressed a strong preference for the automated workflow. MSK leadership now views Archer as part of their standard operating model and has articulated a long-term strategy to transition all eligible studies into the platform. From a sponsor perspective, AstraZeneca has reported a 70% reduction in manual data entry and an 87% reduction in data queries. Johnson & Johnson has established an enterprise contract and is actively scaling Archer across dozens of studies at leading institutions. As Amy Cramer of Johnson & Johnson noted, "We're at the tipping point; with Ignite, we're scaling sites and data to make EHR-to-sponsor the norm." The future of innovation in healthcare Kristen Andrews: What are your plans for future innovations? Zach Taft: Our ultimate intention is to transfer 100% of the data necessary for comprehensive decision-making on clinical trials, across all data domains and data types, both structured and unstructured, spanning all therapeutic areas. Our next major area of innovation is unstructured clinical data, such as clinical notes and imaging. While many companies claim to support unstructured data in clinical trials, delivering the consistency, auditability, and scalability required for regulated research environments is an entirely different challenge. Through close partnerships with leading research sites and sponsors, we’re applying large language models in a targeted way to specific, high-value data types where accuracy, traceability, and repeatability can be validated in real-world environments. This capability will expand incrementally to ensure it meets the rigorous standards required in clinical research, extending Archer's ability to reduce manual effort and unlock deeper clinical insights while maintaining the governance and scalability that underpin the platform today. Kristen Andrews: How do you plan to expand your reach and impact? Zach Taft: Our growth strategy centers on scaling the network while remaining the only genuinely agnostic solution in the market. We’re expanding across more research sites, more sponsors, and more therapeutic areas, deepening the value we deliver within each study. As more data domains flow through our pipelines, we reduce operational friction for both sites and sponsors, which in turn increases site capacity and allows more studies to run in parallel. This creates a reinforcing cycle: Measurable efficiency gains drive broader adoption Broader adoption generates stronger evidence of impact Continuous expansion is supported Ultimately, we aim for this cycle because increased adoption leads to more data, better outcomes, and broader scalability across the clinical research ecosystem. Partnerships play a central role in this strategy. Our collaboration with Labcorp, for example, has the potential to link central laboratory data at scale directly into sponsor EDC systems and back into site workflows, significantly reducing manual reconciliation for research teams. Kristen Andrews: How do you stay ahead of emerging trends in healthcare? Zach Taft: Our most valuable insights come directly from our partners. We sit directly between research sites and sponsors, giving us a real-time view into evolving challenges and opportunities as we have continuous, in-depth conversations about trial execution, data quality, operations, emerging technology, and patient needs. That engagement allows us to identify meaningful trends early and focus our innovation efforts on areas where new technologies can deliver practical, validated impact in clinical research. This constant feedback loop allows us to focus on practical innovation that delivers immediate value, rather than chasing theoretical use cases. Partnering for innovation IgniteData is redefining how clinical data moves across the healthcare ecosystem, removing bottlenecks that slow studies and delay patient access to life-saving treatments. By eliminating manual processes, improving data quality, and accelerating research timelines, they’re enabling health systems, clinicians, and life sciences organizations to operate more efficiently and deliver better outcomes. Through platform-agnostic, regulatory-compliant technology, a rapidly growing network of the world's top research institutions, and a relentless focus on data quality, IgniteData is demonstrating how smarter data automation translates directly into faster studies, lower costs, and better outcomes for patients. Labcorp is proud to support companies like IgniteData that are advancing the infrastructure of clinical research to benefit the entire healthcare ecosystem. Contact Labcorp to access the technology, data, capital, resources, and expertise you need to scale successful innovations. Contact us Subscribe now

body_text: View All News Femasys Strengthens and Extends Global Patent Protection for FemBloc® with First Issued Blended Polymer Patents 08/12/2026 -- New U.S. and international patents complement existing delivery system patents, extending global IP coverage for the FemBloc solution -- ATLANTA, Aug. 12, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Femasys Inc. (NASDAQ: FEMY), a leading biomedical innovator developing transformative fertility and non-surgical permanent birth control solutions designed to improve the standard of care, expand access, and reduce costs for women worldwide, announced today the issuance of patents in the United States and key international markets that expand intellectual property protection for the blended polymer component of FemBloc, the Company’s non-surgical permanent birth control technology. These patents broaden and extend FemBloc’s global intellectual property protection, complementing existing patents covering its delivery system and further strengthening the technology’s competitive position in a highly regulated market with rigorous clinical and regulatory requirements. FemBloc is approved for marketing in Europe and other select international markets and remains investigational in the United States. “Developing a truly new approach to permanent birth control requires overcoming significant scientific, technical and regulatory hurdles,” said Kathy Lee-Sepsick, Chief Executive Officer and Founder of Femasys. “These first issued patents covering the blended polymer extend protection for the FemBloc solution beyond the delivery system and further strengthen the intellectual property foundation supporting this differentiated approach. As we advance FemBloc through the ongoing U.S. pivotal trial, this expanding patent portfolio helps protect the innovation behind FemBloc as we work to bring it to women globally.” FemBloc is a first-of-its-kind, non-surgical solution for permanent birth control, addressing a significant unmet need in women’s reproductive health. The technology combines a patented delivery system with a separately patented blended polymer that is placed into both fallopian tubes, safely degrades and forms natural scar tissue for permanent occlusion. Unlike surgical sterilization, FemBloc requires no anesthesia, incisions or recovery time, offering women a more convenient and affordable alternative while avoiding risks associated with surgery. Together with existing patents covering the delivery system, these patents broaden and extend intellectual property coverage for FemBloc across key global markets. Learn more at www.FemBloc.com . The Company is focused on commercializing its fertility portfolio, led by FemaSeed® Intratubal Insemination, together with complementary diagnostic and sperm preparation products, in the U.S. and key international markets. FemBloc received regulatory approvals in Europe, the UK and New Zealand in 2025, supporting commercialization through strategic partnerships in select international markets. title: Caesars Palace at 60: The Evolution of the Casino Floor
summary: Explore how Caesars Palace shaped the Las Vegas Strip and how slot innovation, TITO, and TransAct Epicentral turned casino floors into revenue engines.
body_text: Sixty years on the Strip Ask anyone who's spent a night working a Vegas floor what a great shift feels like, and they won't start with the tables. They'll talk about the noise. The lights syncing up with the machines. Thousands of little wins landing all at once, all over the room. Sixty years ago this month — August 5, 1966 — one property decided to build that feeling right into the walls. Caesars Palace opened its doors, and the business of Las Vegas hasn't been the same since. That's not an anniversary we wanted to let slide by with a quick mention. It's a good excuse to look back at how one resort helped invent the modern casino experience — and at a quieter shift that happened right alongside it: how the slot floor turned into the engine that funds almost everything else in the building. Jay Sarno's big, weird, brilliant bet Caesars Palace was the brainchild of developer Jay Sarno, who wanted guests to feel like they'd checked into a fantasy, not a hotel room. UNLV history professor Michael Green put it to the Las Vegas Review-Journal for its anniversary coverage : Caesars was really the first luxury-themed resort on the Strip. Sarno was betting that spectacle would sell rooms — and he was right. That one bet reshaped the Strip for decades. Caesars either invented or popularized things that are everywhere now: the Forum Shops, celebrity-chef dining, even the modern superstar residency (yes, we can thank Caesars for eventually giving us Celine Dion on the Strip). Gaming historian David Schwartz, former director of UNLV's Center for Gaming Research, put it better than we could: "Caesars really being the first casino that became a brand rather than just a location." — David Schwartz, gaming historian, former director, UNLV Center for Gaming Research Evel Knievel jumped the fountains there. Sinatra played the showroom. Movies from Rain Man to The Hangover carried the Caesars name to people who'd never set foot in Nevada. Not bad for a 60-year-old building. The machine nobody took seriously Here's the part most anniversary write-ups skip right over. When Caesars opened in 1966, slot machines weren't exactly the main event — they were more of a babysitter, something to keep a spouse busy while the "real" gambling happened at the tables. UNLV's oral history of the industry gives a lot of credit to people like William "Si" Redd, whose company would later become IGT, for dragging slots out of that back seat and turning them into one of the biggest financial engines gaming has ever seen. If you're running a floor today, you already feel how completely that shift took hold. But the numbers are still worth putting in front of you. The American Gaming Association's 2026 State of the States report puts 2025 U.S. slot revenue at $37.13 billion against $10.05 billion from table games — and slots were the only one of the two still growing. Nevada tells the same story on a smaller scale: the state just closed its 2025-26 fiscal year at $16.05 billion in statewide gaming win, up 2.59%, with the Las Vegas Strip alone responsible for $8.95 billion of that. Why? The math isn't complicated. Slots cost less labor per dollar of win, they scale in ways a pit game never will, and they keep quietly earning long after the tables have gone dark for the night. The machine on the floor stopped being a sideshow and became the main event — and it hasn't given that spot back since. The night the coin bucket disappeared The next big leap changed how all that revenue actually moved through the building. For decades, a slot win meant coins clattering into a tray, then lugging a bucket to the cage. That started to change in 2000, when IGT's EZ Pay voucher system got the green light from Nevada regulators after a Las Vegas field trial. Ticket-in, ticket-out — TITO to anyone who's worked a floor — swapped the coin hopper for a barcoded thermal ticket, and it caught on fast. IGT reported shipping more than 20,000 EZ Pay machines within a year of Nevada's approval. For operators, TITO wasn't just a nice convenience upgrade — it changed the job. Hopper fills went away. Machines stayed in play longer between service calls. Cash handling got simpler and a lot safer. It also opened the door to lower denominations and multi-denomination games, which is a big reason the penny slot became such a floor staple. And once a machine could print a ticket, it could print something else, too. A coupon. A bonus offer. A drawing entry — handed to the guest while they're still sitting in the seat. From cash-out ticket to marketing moment By the mid-2000s, the printer had quietly stopped being an accessory bolted onto the side of the machine and started being part of the machine itself. In December 2004, IGT and TransAct signed a supply, sales, and license agreement that made TransAct's Epic 950 a standard option across IGT's slot platforms. Most histories of the Strip won't even give this a footnote, but it's genuinely the moment the ticket printer went from plumbing to product design. That same print head kept evolving from there. A ticket wasn't just a ticket anymore — it could be a coupon, a bonus offer, a drawing entry, delivered in real time while the guest was still playing. That idea became Epicentral , the real-time promotional system TransAct rolled out in 2010, which reaches both carded and un-carded players right at the machine, mid-session. None of this replaces what Jay Sarno understood back in 1966. Guests still come for the experience first, full stop. The technology behind the floor is just there to make that experience feel effortless — and honestly, the best of it is the kind nobody ever notices. Sixty years of reinvention Caesars Palace has outlasted plenty of Strip icons that got imploded and rebuilt, mostly because it never stopped changing. The slot floor's story runs in parallel — mechanical reels to server-based gaming, coin buckets to barcoded tickets to real-time offers delivered mid-session. Both stories teach the same lesson heading into the next sixty years: protect what gets people through the door, and keep investing in what keeps them playing once they're inside. Happy anniversary, Caesars. The house that reset the Strip is still teaching the rest of the industry how it's done. See how TransAct's Epic gaming printers and Epicentral promotional software help operators get more out of every interaction on the floor.

title: Why Work in Japan: Top Reasons to Build Your Career There
summary: Curious about why work in Japan is a dream for so many people? Discover the top reasons Japan is one of the best countries to build your career abroad.
body_text: Have you ever caught yourself scrolling through videos of Tokyo’s neon-lit streets, bullet trains, and perfectly organized convenience stores, thinking, “What would it be like to actually live and work there?” You’re not alone. Japan has become one of the most sought-after destinations for professionals looking to take their careers to the next level. And if you’ve been wondering why work in Japan is such a popular goal, you’re about to find out. The truth is, working in Japan isn’t just about the paycheck or the anime references. It’s about stepping into a culture that genuinely respects hard work, values growth, and offers a quality of life that’s hard to match anywhere else in the world. Let’s break it down. List of Content Toggle Japan’s Job Market Is Actively Welcoming Foreign Workers One of the biggest misconceptions about Japan is that it’s a closed market. In reality, Japan is facing a well-documented labor shortage, and the government has been opening its doors wider than ever to skilled foreign professionals. If you have a marketable skill, Japan genuinely wants you. 1. Growing Demand for Skilled Foreign Talent Industries like IT, engineering, healthcare, education, and finance are actively recruiting from overseas. Companies in Japan are not just tolerating foreign hires; they are building diverse teams and valuing the fresh perspectives that international professionals bring. 2. Visa Pathways Are More Accessible Japan has expanded its visa categories in recent years, including the Highly Skilled Professional Visa and the Specified Skilled Worker program. These are designed to make it easier for qualified candidates to enter the workforce legally and on solid footing. If you’re serious about making the move, this guide on how to work abroad from Indonesia is a great starting point for understanding the process. The Professional Culture in Japan Is Unlike Anywhere Else Working in Japan means immersing yourself in a professional culture built on discipline, precision, and deep mutual respect. It can be challenging at first, but the rewards are enormous for those who embrace it. 1. A Strong Sense of Teamwork and Loyalty Japanese workplaces tend to operate with a strong sense of collective purpose. You’re not just an employee; you’re part of a team working toward a shared goal. This fosters a level of camaraderie and trust that many professionals find deeply satisfying. 2. Commitment to Quality in Everything Japan is famous for its concept of kaizen , the philosophy of continuous improvement. Whether you’re building software or managing a project, the expectation is that you always strive to do it better. Working in this environment naturally sharpens your professional skills faster than most other workplaces. 3. Respect for Work-Life Structure While Japan has historically been associated with long working hours, there has been a significant cultural shift in recent years. Many companies now actively promote work-life balance, paid leave usage, and flexible arrangements, especially in startups and international firms based in Japan. The Financial and Lifestyle Benefits Are Genuinely Compelling Beyond the professional culture, the practical advantages of living and working in Japan are hard to overlook. From safety to infrastructure to the sheer richness of everyday life, Japan offers a standard of living that consistently ranks among the highest in the world. 1. One of the Safest Countries in the World Japan regularly tops global safety rankings. As a foreigner working there, you can walk home late at night, use public transit without worry, and generally feel secure in ways that aren’t always possible in other major cities around the world. That peace of mind alone is worth a lot. 2. World-Class Public Infrastructure Japan’s public transportation system is legendary for a reason. Trains run on time, roads are well-maintained, and the healthcare system is robust and accessible. Day-to-day life is simply efficient, which gives you more mental energy to focus on your career and personal growth. 3. A Rich Cultural Experience Working abroad isn’t just a career move; it’s a life experience. Japan offers a cultural depth that takes years to fully appreciate, from its festivals and seasonal traditions to its food, art, and philosophy. Living there means you get to experience all of this firsthand, not just as a tourist but as a real participant in daily life. Japan Is a Launchpad for Long-Term Career Growth Here’s something people don’t talk about enough: having Japan on your resume is a career accelerator. Employers around the world recognize that working in Japan requires adaptability, cross-cultural communication, and a high level of professional discipline. These are qualities that open doors everywhere. 1. Build a Global Professional Network Japan is home to some of the world’s most influential corporations, including Toyota, Sony, SoftBank, and many others. Working in this environment puts you in proximity to global decision-makers and innovators. The network you build in Japan can follow you throughout your entire career. 2. Language Skills That Set You Apart Learning Japanese, even at a basic conversational level, is a skill that very few professionals outside Japan possess. Even a working knowledge of the language can significantly boost your value in industries that deal with Japanese markets, partners, or clients. It’s an investment that keeps paying off. 3. Transferable Skills Across Industries The discipline, attention to detail, and collaborative mindset you develop while working in Japan translate directly to virtually any industry or country you move to afterward. Many professionals who have worked in Japan describe it as the experience that defined their careers. If you’re weighing your options, it’s also worth reading about how to find a job abroad to understand how to position yourself for roles in competitive international markets like Japan. Practical Things to Know Before You Go Deciding to work in Japan is exciting, but it pays to go in prepared. Here are a few practical things to keep in mind as you plan your move. Learn some Japanese before you arrive. Even basic phrases show respect and make daily life much easier. Understand the work culture. Punctuality, attention to hierarchy, and group harmony are not optional extras; they are core expectations. Sort out your banking early. Setting up a local bank account as soon as you arrive will make managing your finances much smoother. Check out this guide on how to open a bank account abroad to get a head start. Plan for remittances. If you’re supporting family back home, make sure you have a reliable, affordable way to send money internationally. Transfez is a great option for sending money from Japan back to Indonesia quickly and easily. Connect with expat communities. Japan has a vibrant expat community, especially in Tokyo and Osaka. These communities are invaluable for practical advice and emotional support when you’re just getting started. See Also: Why Do So Many Indonesians Work Abroad? Working in Japan is not just a job; it’s a decision that can reshape your perspective, accelerate your growth, and give you stories worth telling for the rest of your life. Whether you’re drawn by the career opportunities, the culture, the lifestyle, or all of the above, Japan has something genuinely special to offer. If you’re ready to make the leap, start planning smart, stay curious, and remember that working in Asia as a foreigner gets easier once you know the right steps to take. title: When Your Accounting Software Blocks AR Automation: A Singapore SME Guide to Integrating Legacy and Local Systems
summary: Using OCI or other local accounting software in Singapore? Learn how to get AR automation without migrating your entire system—layer, don't replace.
body_text: TL;DR: Many Singapore SMEs hit the same wall when exploring AR automation: their accounting vendor tells them “we only integrate with Xero, QuickBooks, or NetSuite”—leaving organizations using locally-developed or niche accounting systems stuck. The solution is not a costly full migration. A layered approach—running an AR automation platform independently from your existing accounting system, connected to an IRSP for InvoiceNow delivery—achieves full AR workflow automation and Peppol compliance in 2 to 5 weeks, without touching your existing finance records. “We Only Integrate With Xero, QuickBooks, or NetSuite.” If you have been exploring AR automation as a Singapore SME using a locally-developed or niche accounting system, you have almost certainly heard some version of this sentence. You reach out to three or four AR automation vendors. Each one asks what accounting software you use. When you name a local system—OCI, or a legacy platform built specifically for the Singapore market—the response is a variation of the same story: integration is not available, custom development would be expensive, or migration to a standard platform is the recommended first step. This is a real barrier. And it affects a substantial number of Singapore organizations. Not every business runs Xero or QuickBooks. Government-linked organizations, legacy businesses, and cost-conscious SMEs often use locally-developed accounting software chosen specifically for its IRAS compliance, local GST handling, or lower subscription costs. These systems work for what they were designed to do. But they were not designed with third-party API integration in mind. The result is an integration gap that effectively blocks these organizations from accessing modern AR automation—unless they know there is another way. This guide explains why the integration gap exists, what it means for AR automation ambitions, and how Singapore SMEs can achieve full AR automation and InvoiceNow compliance through a layered approach—without migrating their entire accounting infrastructure. Why Local Accounting Software Creates an AR Automation Barrier How Most AR Automation Platforms Are Built AR automation platforms are designed to pull invoice data from your accounting system, route it through approval workflows, deliver it to customers, and push payment status back. For this to work seamlessly, the AR platform needs a reliable, structured connection to wherever your invoices live—your accounting system. The most efficient way to build this connection is via API—a direct, real-time data exchange between systems. Global accounting platforms like Xero, QuickBooks, and NetSuite all publish comprehensive APIs with full documentation and established integration ecosystems. This is why AR automation vendors build for these platforms first and often exclusively. Why Local Systems Are Different Locally-developed accounting software in Singapore was typically built to address specific local requirements: IRAS GST filing, local payroll integration, UEN-based record keeping. These systems were designed in an era when software was self-contained rather than interconnected. As a result: Most do not publish external APIs Data is stored in proprietary formats not designed for third-party access Export capabilities are limited to specific report formats (often PDF or basic CSV) Vendor support for integration requests is limited or expensive When an AR automation vendor says they “only integrate with Xero, QuickBooks, or NetSuite,” they are not being arbitrary. They are describing a genuine technical constraint: without a published API or standardized data structure, building and maintaining a reliable integration requires expensive custom development that may not be commercially viable for the vendor to offer. The Cost of Custom Integration Organizations that pursue custom integration between a local accounting system and an AR automation platform face significant cost and complexity: Custom integration development: SGD 8,000–30,000 (one-time) Ongoing maintenance when either system updates: SGD 2,000–8,000 per year Integration project timeline: 2–6 months Risk of integration breaking when the accounting software releases updates For most Singapore SMEs, this cost is prohibitive—especially when the entire motivation for AR automation is to reduce operational cost and inefficiency. Integration Approach Typical Cost (SGD) Timeline Risk Level Standard API (Xero/QuickBooks/NetSuite) Included in platform subscription 1–3 weeks Low Custom API development (local system) 8,000–30,000 one-time 2–6 months Medium–High File-based export/import Low (configuration only) 1–2 weeks Low Layered platform (independent of existing system) Included in platform subscription 2–4 weeks Low Full accounting system migration 10,000–50,000+ 3–9 months High Three Paths Forward—and Why Layering Wins for Most Singapore SMEs Path 1: Migrate to a Standard Accounting Platform The cleanest long-term solution is migrating your accounting operations to an IRSP-certified platform like Xero or QuickBooks. Once on a standard platform, all major AR automation tools will integrate natively. The reality: A full accounting migration is a major operational undertaking. It involves migrating historical data, re-training your finance team, reconfiguring your chart of accounts, and managing a transition period where two systems run in parallel. For most Singapore SMEs, this is a 3–9 month project requiring significant internal resource commitment—far more than most organizations can manage while continuing to run day-to-day operations. When this makes sense: If your organization is already planning a broader digital transformation or is implementing a new ERP, bundling accounting system migration with AR automation is logical. For all other cases, the cost and disruption typically do not justify migration as a first step. Path 2: Custom Integration Commission a custom integration between your local accounting system and an AR automation platform. The reality: As outlined above, custom integration costs are significant, timelines are long, and ongoing maintenance is a recurring expense. Unless your local accounting system has some data export capability that reduces the integration complexity, this path is rarely cost-effective for SMEs. When this makes sense: If your organization has technical resources, a long-term commitment to your existing accounting platform, and invoice volumes high enough to justify the investment—and if your accounting system has some form of data export capability to reduce development cost. Path 3: Layer an AR Automation Platform (Recommended for Most SMEs) The layered approach treats AR automation as a function that runs alongside your existing accounting system rather than through it. Here is how it works: Your existing accounting system continues to be your system of record for GL, tax, payroll, and financial reporting A separate AR automation platform handles all outgoing invoice processes: creation, approval routing, InvoiceNow delivery, customer reminders, and collections Invoice data is transferred from your existing system to the AR platform via scheduled file export (CSV or Excel) or manual entry for low-volume scenarios For InvoiceNow compliance, the AR platform connects to an IRSP (such as Xero used as a transmission layer) to send Peppol-network invoices to government customers Payment confirmations received by the AR platform are manually reconciled or exported back to your accounting system Why this works: The layered approach acknowledges that your existing accounting system does not need to be replaced to achieve AR automation. Invoice approval, InvoiceNow delivery, automated customer reminders, and AR reporting can all function effectively as a separate workflow layer. Your accounting system continues to handle what it is good at—financial record keeping—while the AR platform handles what requires automation. What the Layered AR Automation Workflow Looks Like in Practice Consider a Singapore organization using a locally-developed accounting system for day-to-day finance operations. They have government agency customers requiring InvoiceNow-compliant invoice delivery and an internal governance requirement for two-level invoice approval before any invoice goes out. Under the layered approach: Step 1 — Invoice creation. The preparer creates the invoice in the AR automation platform (or exports invoice data from the existing accounting system via CSV and imports it into the platform as a batch). Step 2 — Automated approval routing. The AR platform routes the invoice to Approver 1 with an automated notification. Approver 1 reviews and approves via the platform’s mobile-friendly interface. The invoice auto-routes to Approver 2. Both approvals are logged with timestamps in the platform’s audit trail. Step 3 — InvoiceNow delivery. Once the final approval is received, the AR platform transmits the invoice electronically to the government customer’s Peppol ID via the connected IRSP (Xero). A delivery confirmation is recorded in the platform. Step 4 — Payment tracking and reminders. The AR platform tracks the invoice against payment due date. If payment is not received by a configured trigger (e.g., 3 days before due date), an automated reminder goes to the customer’s finance contact. Step 5 — Reconciliation. When payment arrives, the finance team updates the payment record in the existing accounting system (manually or via export from the AR platform) to close the invoice. The key insight: steps 1 through 4 require no integration with the existing accounting system. The AR automation layer operates independently. Only step 5 touches the existing system—and that step remains manual, just as it would be without AR automation. For organizations wanting to understand the full impact of invoice delivery gaps on working capital , this architecture resolves the delivery bottleneck entirely, even when the underlying accounting system cannot integrate. InvoiceNow Compliance via the Layered Approach One of the most important benefits of the layered approach is that it provides a clear path to InvoiceNow compliance for AR without requiring your existing accounting software to be IRSP-certified. In this architecture: Your existing accounting system is not InvoiceNow-ready (that is the problem) Your AR automation platform connects to Xero as an IRSP transmission layer (not as your accounting system) When invoices are approved and ready for delivery in the AR platform, they are transmitted via Xero to the government customer’s Peppol ID Xero is used solely as the Peppol network access point—it is not your general ledger, your financial reporting tool, or your tax filing system This means a Xero subscription in this architecture is a narrow-function cost—essentially paying for InvoiceNow network access—rather than a full accounting platform migration. The total cost of a Xero subscription for this purpose is a fraction of a full migration project. For organizations that also need to strengthen their internal AR invoice approval workflow before invoices reach government customers, the layered platform handles both approval and delivery in a single flow. How Peakflo Enables the Layered Approach Peakflo’s Invoice-to-Cash Automation platform is designed to operate as a standalone AR layer that connects to an IRSP for InvoiceNow delivery—without requiring your existing accounting system to integrate. Key capabilities relevant to organizations with local accounting software: Independent invoice management. Invoices can be created directly in Peakflo without requiring a real-time connection to your existing accounting system. For organizations with CSV export capability, invoices can be imported in batch. Xero IRSP integration. Peakflo integrates with Xero as an InvoiceNow-ready service provider. Organizations can use this integration purely for Peppol network delivery—keeping Xero as a transmission layer rather than their primary accounting platform. Multi-step approval workflow. Configurable sequential or parallel approval chains with automated notifications, reminders, and escalation. Full audit trail for each invoice regardless of what accounting system sits behind the platform. Automated customer reminders. Once invoices are delivered, Peakflo tracks payment status and sends automated reminders via email or WhatsApp at configurable intervals—reducing manual collections follow-up. PSG grant eligibility. Peakflo is a PSG pre-approved vendor. Singapore SMEs using the layered approach can receive up to 50% co-funding via the Productivity Solutions Grant —covering the AR automation platform cost even if the underlying accounting system is not PSG-approved. For broader context on Singapore’s finance and ERP integration landscape , the layered approach is increasingly standard practice for organizations bridging legacy systems and modern automation requirements. Our Verdict: Should You Replace, Layer, or Integrate? Choose Layering if: Your existing accounting software lacks a published API You do not have plans to migrate your accounting system in the next 12 months Your primary need is AR workflow automation (approvals, InvoiceNow delivery, collections)—not replacing your financial reporting system You want the fastest path to InvoiceNow compliance for government agency customers You want to qualify for PSG grant funding with minimal disruption Choose Migration if: You are already planning a digital transformation or ERP upgrade Your existing accounting system has significant limitations beyond the AR integration gap (poor GST support, inadequate reporting, scalability issues) You have the internal resources and timeline to manage a 3–9 month migration project Choose Custom Integration if: Your existing accounting system has usable export capabilities that reduce integration development scope Your invoice volumes are high enough to justify the custom integration investment You have in-house technical resources who can maintain the integration over time Our Recommendation: For the majority of Singapore SMEs using locally-developed or niche accounting software, the layered approach is the fastest, most cost-effective, and least operationally disruptive path to AR automation and InvoiceNow compliance. Start with the AR automation layer; migrate your accounting system if and when a broader business need justifies it—not as a prerequisite for automation. Conclusion A locally-developed accounting system should not be a permanent barrier to AR automation. The “we only integrate with Xero or QuickBooks” response from AR automation vendors reflects a real technical constraint—but it does not mean the only answer is a costly, time-consuming migration. The layered approach unlocks AR automation, InvoiceNow compliance, and multi-step invoice approval workflows in weeks rather than months—using your existing accounting system as the financial record keeper it was always designed to be, while a dedicated AR platform handles everything your customers see on the way to getting paid. If you are a Singapore SME navigating this integration challenge, request a demo of Peakflo to see how the layered AR automation approach works in practice for organizations with local accounting systems. Frequently Asked Questions Why can’t most AR automation platforms integrate with local Singapore accounting software? Most AR automation platforms build integrations for globally-standardized accounting systems (Xero, QuickBooks, NetSuite, SAP) that publish APIs. Locally-developed accounting software typically lacks published APIs or uses proprietary data formats, making standard integration unavailable without expensive custom development. Do I have to migrate my accounting software to get AR automation? No. A layered approach runs an AR automation platform independently from your existing system, using file-based data transfer or batch import for invoice data. This avoids full migration while delivering AR automation and InvoiceNow compliance. What is the difference between replacing and layering an AR automation system? Replacing means migrating all finance operations to a new system. Layering adds an AR automation platform for specific functions (approval, delivery, collections) while your existing accounting system remains the system of record. Can I achieve InvoiceNow compliance without migrating to Xero or QuickBooks? Yes. By connecting an AR automation platform to Xero purely as an IRSP transmission layer, invoices can be delivered to government customers via Peppol without Xero being your primary accounting system. What is a file-based integration and can it work for AR automation? A file-based integration transfers data via structured files (CSV, Excel) exported from one system and imported into another. For AR automation, a daily CSV export of new invoices from your existing system into the AR platform is sufficient for most workflow automation needs. How much does custom integration of a local accounting system cost? Custom integration typically costs SGD 8,000–30,000 one-time, plus SGD 2,000–8,000 per year for maintenance. For most Singapore SMEs, the layered approach is significantly more cost-effective. Can I get PSG grant funding even if my accounting software is not PSG-approved? Yes. The PSG grant covers the cost of the new pre-approved AR automation solution you are adopting—it does not require your existing accounting software to be PSG-approved. What happens to historical invoice data when I layer an AR automation platform? Your existing accounting system retains all historical data. The AR automation platform handles new invoices going forward. Open receivables can optionally be imported as a one-time batch for collections visibility. Is there an IMDA-approved path for organizations using local accounting software? Yes. You can adopt a PSG pre-approved AR automation platform regardless of your existing system. The AR platform connects to an IRSP for InvoiceNow compliance—creating an IMDA-compliant path without changing your underlying accounting software. How long does setup take with the layered approach? Most Singapore SMEs can complete layered AR automation setup in 2 to 5 weeks—covering approval workflow configuration, IRSP connection for InvoiceNow, customer record setup, and pilot testing. Running local accounting software and exploring AR automation? Request a demo of Peakflo to see how the layered approach works for Singapore organizations with niche or legacy accounting systems.

body_text: Manual medical record retrieval can take weeks or months, and in a personal injury practice that lag shows up directly in case velocity. This checklist covers the HIPAA authorization elements, Miami healthcare system contacts, and submission procedures PI lawyers need to get complete records without the back-and-forth. Platforms like Codes Health work toward complete, organized records in a couple of weeks through AI-assisted request validation, persistent provider follow-up, and completeness verification before delivery. Key Takeaways HIPAA generally requires a covered entity to act within 30 calendar days on a qualifying right-of-access request, with one possible 30-day extension. Attorney requests made under a separate HIPAA authorization do not carry that federal deadline, and state deadlines may be shorter Codes Health identifies incomplete or defective authorizations as a leading cause of provider rejection, since missing signatures, unclear expiration dates, and unaddressed sensitive-record categories send you back to the start Major Miami facilities each run their own procedures, and Jackson Health System maintains a dedicated attorney workflow separate from patient requests Florida licensed hospitals may generally charge no more than $1.00 per page for paper records under state law, subject to that statute's other terms and any federal right-of-access limits Patient portals such as MyChart, myJacksonHealth, and MyHealthONE help with preliminary review, but facilities warn that some records are only available through the medical records office Codes Health's AI platform validates authorizations before submission, manages persistent provider follow-up, and works toward organized records in a couple of weeks rather than months, on a flat fee Understanding the HIPAA Authorization Form for Medical Records in Personal Injury Cases For a PI firm seeking a client's records through a voluntary third-party disclosure, a valid authorization is typically required unless another legal basis applies. Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule , providers need valid written authorization before releasing protected health information to third parties like law firms. Keep the two pathways straight. A patient's own right-of-access request under Section 164.524 carries a federal response deadline. A disclosure on a conventional authorization under Section 164.508 is a permitted disclosure, and HHS has said HIPAA imposes no comparable timeliness requirement there. Most attorney requests take the authorization path, so planning a calendar around a guaranteed federal clock leaves you exposed. Key Elements of a Valid HIPAA Authorization An authorization must contain all core elements and required statements under Section 164.508, including: Description of the information : specific record types, such as treatment notes, billing, and imaging Authorized disclosure party : the provider releasing records Authorized recipient : your firm's name and contact information Purpose statement : for example, personal injury litigation Expiration date or event : a specific date or triggering event Patient signature and date : original or valid electronic signature Required statements : notice of the right to revoke, whether treatment or payment can be conditioned on the authorization, and the potential for redisclosure Separately from HIPAA's mandatory elements, facilities routinely ask for identifiers that help them locate the right chart: date of birth, medical record number, current address, and sometimes the last four of a Social Security number. These are provider requirements, not statutory ones, which is why the same form sails through at one hospital and stalls at another. Avoiding Common Pitfalls with HIPAA Forms Codes Health identifies incomplete or defective authorizations as a leading cause of provider rejection. Common errors that restart your retrieval clock include: Missing patient signatures or dates Incomplete handling of specially protected information such as mental health, HIV and STD, or substance use records Expired authorization dates Insufficient identifying information for common names Missing representative documentation for deceased patients or minors Requests involving specially protected information may require additional consent language or provider-specific documentation under federal or Florida law. Substance use records from covered programs, for example, fall under 42 C.F.R. Part 2, whose revised consent requirements became mandatory in February 2026. Treating every sensitive category as a checkbox on a generic form is how requests come back unfulfilled. Codes Health uses AI-assisted validation to review requests before submission, flagging misspellings, missing dates of service, and signature issues that would otherwise cause provider rejections. Essential Medical Records Release Forms: Templates and Best Practices for Miami PI Lawyers Beyond standard HIPAA authorizations, keep facility-specific forms on hand for the major Miami healthcare systems. Customizing Release Forms for Specific Case Needs University of Miami Health System provides two downloadable forms in English, Spanish, and Creole : Attachment 19 : Request for Access to Health Information, used for patient requests for their own records Authorization for 3rd Party Disclosure : the form attorneys should normally use when proceeding under the authorization pathway Nicklaus Children's Hospital requires additional signatures for psychiatry and psychology, HIV and STD, drug screen, and pregnancy records. Patients age 18 and older authorize their own records regardless of a parent's prior consent. Ensuring Complete Information on Your Release Forms Every authorization should specify: Exact date ranges for requested records All record types needed: medical, billing, imaging, and pharmacy Departments involved, such as emergency, specialists, and primary care Format preference, with electronic delivery usually cheaper and faster Codes Health provides a HIPAA-compliant e-signature workflow for intake documents, including releases of information and authorization forms. Overcoming Delays in Medical Record Acquisition The cadence below is an internal practice recommendation, not a statutory timetable, since most attorney requests are not governed by HIPAA's individual access deadline: First week : phone follow-up confirming receipt and whether anything is missing Second week : written follow-up to a supervisor, restating the request scope Third week : escalate to the compliance officer or patient advocate Fourth week : formal demand letter with delivery confirmation When voluntary retrieval stalls : if the case permits formal discovery, counsel can evaluate subpoena procedures under the Florida Rules of Civil Procedure Codes Health manages follow-up across calls, faxes, emails, and portals until records reach your firm, which takes the tracking spreadsheet off your paralegal's desk entirely. Requesting Archived Records from Closed Practices When providers have closed or merged: Check with the state medical board for successor practice information Review explanation of benefits statements for accurate facility names Contact hospital systems that may have acquired the practice Codes Health custodian connections , patient portals, and traditional channels help identify where records exist across multiple facilities Ensuring Completeness: A Checklist for Medical Record Retrieval in Personal Injury Cases Receiving records is only halfway. Verifying completeness is what prevents trial surprises. Identifying Gaps in Retrieved Medical Records Review each delivery for: Date range coverage : all requested dates included without gaps Record type completeness : treatment notes, billing, imaging, and labs Billing records : these often require separate requests Imaging media : discs or files enclosed, not just radiology reports Legibility : no cutoff pages or unreadable sections What to Do When Records Are Incomplete Codes Health verifies completeness against the original request before delivery. When records appear incomplete, it works with the facility to resolve the gaps before returning the completed set to your firm. This analysis is tailored to specific practice areas instead of producing generic summaries. The Bottom Line for Miami PI Firms Most records problems in a Miami PI practice are not bad luck. They are preventable failure modes that repeat until the process changes.
